Surah 111: Al-Masad (The Palm Fiber)

Meccan, and its number of verses is five.

﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾, that is: were ruined. He is ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. The choice of "perish" (tabb) over "ruin" (halak), and its attribution to his two hands, is because of what has been narrated: when the verse "And warn your closest kindred" (26:214) was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) climbed al-Ṣafā and gathered his relatives and warned them. Abu Lahab said: "Ruin to you! Is it for this that you summoned us?" and he took a stone to throw at him (peace be upon him) with it. ﴿And he perished﴾, that is: and he, all of him, was ruined. It was also said: what is meant by the first is the ruin of his whole person, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ (2:195). The meaning of "and he perished" is: that occurred and came to pass, like the saying of one who said:

She has repaid me, may Allah repay her with the worst of her repayments, the repayment of the ravenous dogs, and she has done it.

This is supported by the reading of those who read "and he has indeed perished" (qad tabba). It was also said: the first is a report about the ruin of his deeds, since deeds are mostly carried out by the hands, and the second is a report about the ruin of himself. It was also said: both are a supplication against him for ruin. It was also said: the first is a supplication and the second is a report. Mentioning his kunya (nickname) is to allude to his being a people of Hell (Jahannami), and because he was well known by it, and because of disliking the mention of his ugly name. It was also read "Abu Lahab" as is said, ʿAlī ibn Abū Ṭālib, and it was read "Abī Lahb" with the ha' sukūn.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 111, verse 2:

﴿What his wealth availed him not, nor what he earned﴾. That is: it did not avail him when the ruin (al-tabab) befell him, according to the reading in which "ma" is a negation; or, "what" availed him, according to the reading in which it is interrogative, carrying the sense of denial, and in the accusative governed by what follows it. The original sense of "his wealth" and "what he earned" is: the profits, results and gains, along with prestige and followers; or his inherited wealth from his father and what he earned by himself; or his wicked deed, which is his scheming in enmity against the Prophet ﷺ; or his deed which he thought was of some worth, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We shall turn to what they did of deeds, and make them scattered dust﴾. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "what his son earned." It is also reported that he used to say: "If what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself from it with my wealth and my children, and so be freed from it." But his hope failed, and he did not obtain what he wished. A lion seized his son 'Utbah on the road to Syria, among the caravan that surrounded him. The Prophet ﷺ had invoked against him, saying: "O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs." He died of the plague (al-'adasah) seven nights after the Battle of Badr, so his family kept away from him for fear of contagion, for Quraysh used to guard against it as they guard against the plague. He remained for three days until he stank. Then they hired some of the Sudanese, who carried him and buried him. So it was (p-211)

the matter as the Qur'an had reported.

﴿He will burn﴾ with a fatha on the yā' (يَ). It has also been read with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fatḥah on the lām, both with light and with heavy (tashdīd) pronunciation. The sīn (س) serves to emphasise and intensify the threat (wa'īd, warning of punishment), meaning: he will certainly enter, without doubt, after this hasty punishment, in the Hereafter, ﴿into a fire of blazing flame﴾, meaning a great fire possessing kindling and blazing. This is the Fire of Jahannam (Hell). This is not an explicit text (naṣṣ) that he will never believe, such that whoever is obligated to faith in the Qur'an would be obligated to believe that he will never believe, and thus be commanded to combine two contradictories (naqīḍayn), as is well known. For the people of the Fire (ṣilliyy al-nār) are not exclusive to the disbelievers, so it is possible for Abu Lahab to understand from this that his entry into the Fire is for his wickedness and sins, not for his disbelief. Therefore there is no necessity for the well-known answer, that what he was obligated to is faith in everything the Prophet (ﷺ) brought in general, not faith in the details of what the Qur'an stated, to the point that he would have to be obligated to believe in his own continuous non-belief.

﴿And his wife﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the pronoun hidden in "will burn" (sayaṣlā), the separation being made by the object (al-mafʿūl). She was Umm Jamil bint Harb, the sister of Abu Sufyan. She used to carry a bundle of thorns, thistles and saʿdan (a thorny plant), and scatter it at night on the path of the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) would walk over it as one walks on silk. It is also said: she used to go about spreading gossip (al-namima). It is said of one who goes about with tale-bearing and sows discord among people that he "carries firewood among them" (yaḥmilu al-ḥaṭab baynahum), meaning he kindles fire among them.

﴿The carrier of firewood﴾ is in the accusative (naṣb) as an expression of reproach and censure (ʿalā al-shatm wa al-dhamm). It is also said that it is in the accusative of state (ḥāliyya), on the basis that the genitive construction is not a true one (ghayr ḥaqīqiyya), since the meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection she will carry a bundle of the firewood of Hell, like zaqqūm and ḍarīʿ.

It is related from Qatada that, despite her great wealth, she used to carry firewood on her back out of extreme stinginess; so she was reproached for stinginess, and the accusative in that case is necessarily one of reproach.

It is also read in the nominative, as a predicate, with "his wife" as the subject (mubtadaʾ). It is read "ḥammālatun" with tanwin, in both the accusative and the nominative, for "firewood" (lil-ḥaṭab) as well. And it is read "Murayyatuhu," in the diminutive, for belittlement (lil-taḥqīr).

In her neck is a rope of palm-fiber (masad). This is a clause made up of a prepositional phrase fronted as predicate and a postponed subject, and the clause is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāliyyah). It was also said: the prepositional phrase is the predicate of "imra'atuhu" (his wife), and "ḥablun" (rope) is raised by it as the agent (fā'iliyyah). It was also said: it is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from "imra'atuhu," on the basis that it is coordinated with the pronoun in "sayaṣlā" (he will burn), and "ḥablun" is the agent, as mentioned. "Al-masad" is what is twisted from ropes with strong twisting, made from the fiber of the doum palm (muql). It was also said: from any fiber whatsoever. It was also said: from the bark of a tree in Yemen. It may also be from the hides of camels and their wool. The meaning is: in her neck is a rope of what has been twisted from rope, and that she carries that bundle of thorns and ties it around her neck, as woodcutters do, to demean her condition and to portray her in the form of some of the firewood-gatherers of the lowly, so that she would be humiliated by that and her husband would be humiliated, while they were in a house of honor and nobility. Murrah al-Hamdani said: Umm Jamil would come every day with a bundle of thorny brush and cast it on the path of the Muslims. One night, while she was carrying a bundle that had exhausted her, she sat down on a stone to rest, and the angel pulled her from behind, and she was strangled by her own rope.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the Surah of al-Masad, 'Perish,' I hope that Allah will not gather him and Abu Lahab in one house."
